Standing arithmetic. All-in = hammer × 1.25 online premium × 1.055 Maine sales tax = hammer × 1.32. Phone or absentee is 20% premium, so × 1.27. No resale exemption — the tax always applies. Metal prices above are deliberately below market so a bid that clears on paper still clears if metals slip before 28 August.
How I arrived at the value numbers — read this before trusting them
My market estimate
My own estimate of what the lot would realistically fetch today in a retail or well-attended auction setting -- not the house estimate, which on this sale runs ahead of the market in several categories. A range, because condition questions are still open on most of these.
If you resold it
What the buyer would actually NET if they had to let it go: regional auction hammer less a 20-25% seller's commission, or a refiner's 87% on melt-grade metal, or private/eBay net where that is the better route. This is the number the brief's real question turns on -- 'if I ever had to let it go, what do I lose?'
Melt values
Weights are MY ESTIMATES from the form and the photographs. The scraped meta.json carries no weights and no descriptions, so not one figure here is a catalogued weight. Every one needs the scale at preview before it is treated as fact. Rates are the brief's deliberately conservative working spot; refiner net is 87%, the middle of the 85-90% band.
Stones
Secondary-market reality, not replacement value. Small melee diamonds, and coloured stones of this era that are routinely heat-treated or synthetic, recover very little on resale -- typically 10-30% of retail and often less. Where a stone is likely a doublet or composite it is called out.
Margin at target
The midpoint of my market range minus the all-in cost at my target bid. Positive means you are buying under market after premium and tax; negative means you are paying up for it. Sort by this to rank the whole list on value rather than on my verdict. Deliberately blank where my market range spans more than three-fold — that width is unresolved uncertainty (a medium, a period, a print process), not value, and averaging it would float the least-known lots to the top of the ranking.
Category and period
Hand-set on the 127 written-up lots. On the 1,373 bulk-screened lots they are assigned automatically from the catalogue title, so treat those as a rough index rather than a considered judgement. Value estimates are NOT given for screened lots — I have not analysed them individually and will not put a number on something I have not looked at.

Standing caution on ivory. This sale carries a great deal of whale’s tooth, walrus, sailor-made and carved elephant ivory. Federal Endangered Species Act and Marine Mammal Protection Act rules restrict what can be done with these afterwards and the documentation will not accompany lots at this price. That is why resale on ivory-content lots is marked well below market.

Lot 2068Day 2

18TH C. PINE SEA CHEST

18th c. · Catalogued · antique
Marine & whalingGeorgian / 18th c.True antiqueMarine
STRONG BUY
key lot

An 18th-century pine sea chest at $300-500 is the best value-per-criterion lot in Day 2. It is catalogued to the 18th century, so the house has committed; it is a genuine maritime object rather than a decorative one; and sea chests are the furniture form most closely tied to the coastal Maine story. At this estimate it is cheaper than most reproduction blanket chests.

Problems. Check the construction before the paint: hand-cut dovetails with visible scribe lines, irregular pit-saw or up-and-down saw marks on the interior, and shrinkage that has pulled the boards out of square all confirm the date. Circular saw marks anywhere mean it is not 18th century. Original becket handles are usually gone; replaced rope beckets are acceptable and normal. Look for a fitted till and for old, dry paint rather than a decorative repaint.

CIRCA 1910 MODEL SAILING SHIP L.F. CHASE, ROCKLAND, MAINE

A circa-1910 model of the sailing ship L.F. Chase of Rockland, Maine is exactly what the brief means by hyper-local material with a small but committed regional audience. It names a specific midcoast port twelve miles from Thomaston and a specific identified vessel, and it is catalogued to a date that sits right on the antique line. Named-vessel Maine models do not come round often.

Problems. Sits on the 1926 line rather than safely behind it, so treat the age claim as borderline rather than settled. Models suffer -- check the rigging is original rather than restrung, that no spars are replaced, and whether the case is period. A model that has been restored is a decorative object; one with its original dusty rigging intact is a document.

Lot 2118Day 2

MAINE REDWARE JUG, ATTRIB. TO MATTHIAS NORCROSS

19th c. · Inferred · antique
Ceramics & vasesFederal / early 19th c.Maine coastalTrue antique
STRONG BUY
key lot

Maine redware attributed to Matthias Norcross is genuinely scarce material. Maine had comparatively few potteries and their output is thinly represented in collections, so attributed pieces carry real interest with the New England redware collectors and with the state historical market simultaneously. At $500-700 this is fairly priced for something that is both antique and locally significant.

Problems. Attributed is the word to watch -- it is an argument, not a fact, and Maine redware attributions are often made on regional characteristics rather than a mark. Ask what the attribution rests on. Redware is soft and chips readily; check the rim and base for losses and for restoration, which is common and often well hidden under paint.

Lot 2139Day 2

C.F. HOPF, KENNEBUNK, ME GRAIN PAINTED STAND

19th c. · Inferred · antique
Furniture & boxesVictorian / 19th c.Maine coastalTrue antique
STRONG BUY
key lot

A grain-painted stand signed or attributed to C.F. Hopf of Kennebunk, Maine at $300-400 is the sort of lot this brief was written to find. Maine-made painted furniture with a named town is doubly documented, grain painting is the decorative surface the folk-art market actually pays for, and the estimate is a fraction of what the same object makes when a Portland dealer describes it properly.

Problems. Original grain paint versus later decoration is the entire value question. Period graining shows through-wear on the top and edges, has settled into an even mellow tone, and the paint has cracked with the wood rather than over it. Check the top is original to the base and that the stand has not been reduced in height, which is common.

Lot 2194Day 2

(28 PCS) CHINESE EXPORT PORCELAIN WITH GILT DECORATION, 19TH CENTURY

c.1800-1820 · Catalogued · antique
Ceramics & vasesGeorgian / 18th c.True antique
STRONG BUY
key lot

Twenty-eight pieces of Chinese export blue and white with gilt, catalogued as 19th century. The photographs argue earlier: a drum-form teapot with domed lid and gilt finial, a matching covered sugar, handleless tea bowls AND handled coffee cans in the same service, and a spearhead-and-cell border of a type that belongs to c.1790-1820 rather than late Qing. The close-up of a saucer shows hand-painted underglaze cobalt with visible brush modulation -- not transfer -- and a gilt rim worn from use rather than fresh. A complete matched export tea service of this date and this many pieces is a $1,200-2,500 lot; the teapot alone is $300-500. At $500-700 the house has catalogued it as generic export china and priced it by the piece. Best straight value in the ceramics.

Problems. Twenty-eight pieces means twenty-eight chances for a chip, a hairline or a stained crack, and the group shot cannot rule any of that out -- lift each saucer at preview and check foot rims and cup handles. Gilt is already worn in places; that is honest age, not damage, but it is where the piece looks tired. Two dish forms appear to be replacements from a near-matching service, which is normal in a survivor of this size but should be counted. Nothing here is marked, so the date rests on form and border, not a stamp.

Lot 2243Day 2

1652 EDITION "ANATOMY OF MELANCHOLY" ROBERT BURTON (1577-1640)

1652 · Catalogued · antique
Books, maps & ephemera17th c. & earlierTrue antique
STRONG BUY
key lot

A 1652 edition of Burton's Anatomy of Melancholy at $500-700. This is a 17th-century book of genuine literary standing -- one of the monuments of English prose -- at a price that reflects the fact that most auction rooms do not have a rare-book bidder in them. Comfortably antique by nearly three centuries, and unlike most objects in this sale it will still be exactly what it is in another three.

Problems. Condition dominates early book values. Check the collation for completeness, particularly the engraved title page, which is the leaf most often missing or supplied in facsimile. Look at the binding -- a period calf binding, even worn, is far preferable to a 19th-century rebind. Damp-staining and worming are usual; loose or detached boards are common and repairable.

Lot 2295Day 2

17TH C. CARVED OAK BIBLE BOX

17th c. · Catalogued · antique
Furniture & boxes17th c. & earlierTrue antique
STRONG BUY
key lot

A carved oak bible box catalogued to the 17th century at $500-700 is remarkable value in absolute terms -- this is an object older than almost anything else in the sale, and the price is that of a middling piece of Victoriana. Bible boxes are the entry point into genuine 17th-century oak and they are portable, useful and durable in a way that most early furniture is not.

Problems. The category is heavily faked and, more often, heavily improved: plain period boxes are carved later to raise their value. Look at the carving's wear pattern -- period carving is worn smooth on the high points and dirty in the recesses, later carving is crisp and clean-cut with bright wood in the grounds. Check for a replaced lid and modern hinges, both of which are near-universal and only moderately damaging.

Lot 2300Day 2

GEORGE III STERLING TANKARD BY WILLIAM CRIPPS

c.1750-1770 · Inferred · antique
Silver & goldGeorgian / 18th c.Precious metalTrue antiqueNamed maker
STRONG BUY
key lot

This is the best sterling proposition in the sale. William Cripps was a first-rank London silversmith working from the 1740s into the 1760s, and the photographs show a proper period baluster mug -- swelling body, moulded spreading foot, double-scroll handle with a leaf-capped upper terminal. It is comfortably antique, it is a documented named maker, and unlike almost everything else in the silver sections the melt floor sits close underneath the estimate rather than far below it. A pint mug of this form runs 10 to 14 troy ounces, which is roughly $460 to $650 of sterling at the working spot before a refiner's cut.

Problems. Called a tankard but shown with no lid, so it is a mug -- do not pay tankard money. The surface carries heavy directional polishing scratches, which on Georgian silver often means a crest or armorial has been buffed out; that thins the body and is the one condition problem that genuinely matters. Check the hallmarks are crisp rather than worn soft, check for a repaired handle joint at the lower terminal, and hold it up to the light for thin spots.

Lot 2398Day 2

GIOVANNI BAPTISTA PIRANESI (ITALY, 1720-1778)

c.1745-1778 · Inferred · antique
Prints & works on paperGeorgian / 18th c.True antiqueNamed maker
STRONG BUY
key lot

Giovanni Battista Piranesi at $500-800 -- and a second at 2399 for the same money. This is the best antique-plus-named-maker combination inside the band anywhere in the sale. Piranesi's Vedute di Roma and Carceri etchings are 18th-century originals by one of the greatest printmakers who ever worked, they are properly catalogued in Hind and Focillon, and lifetime impressions still trade in the low thousands. At $500-800 either these are later Firmin-Didot restrikes, or the house has underestimated them.

Problems. Establish which. Lifetime impressions show a crisp plate mark, heavy inky burr in the shadows, and period laid paper with a Roman watermark. The 19th-century Firmin-Didot and 20th-century Calcografia restrikes are printed from the same worn plates on whiter, smoother paper and are worth $150-400 -- still a fair buy at $500 but not the same object. Check margins for trimming, which is the standard fault.

Lot 3347Day 3

CARROLL THAYER BERRY (ME, 1886-1978)

c.1930-1960 · Inferred · modern
Prints & works on paperMid-centuryMaine coastalNamed maker
STRONG BUY
key lot

The photographs confirm this is the real thing and it is the best Maine buy in the sale. It is a genuine Carroll Thayer Berry colour woodblock of Bass Harbor Light on the Maine coast, pencil-titled BASS HARBOR LIGHT - MAINE COAST along the lower margin, pencil-signed Carroll Thayer Berry at the right and annotated 'imp' -- meaning he pulled the impression himself rather than having it printed commercially. The cut CTB monogram is in the block at lower left. The green-and-black two-block scheme is his characteristic palette. This earns its place on regional desirability rather than age, exactly as the brief allows, and Bass Harbor Light is one of the most recognisable subjects on the coast.

Problems. There is visible foxing -- scattered orange-brown spots through the sky and into the margins. That is the condition-discount opportunity in its purest form: the market marks foxed paper down hard, but at normal viewing distance on a wall it reads as age rather than damage. Do check whether the spots are surface foxing or have gone through the sheet, and be aware the mat is likely acidic and should be replaced. The frame is a plain mid-century gilt moulding, adequate but not adding value.

(3) EARLY MASSACHUSETTS PORCELAIN LICENSE PLATES, 1904–1909

1904-1909 · Catalogued · antique
Ceramics & vasesEdwardian / c.1900-1920True antique

Three early Massachusetts porcelain-enamel automobile plates: two of the 'MASS. AUTOMOBILE REGISTER' type (numbers 12478 and 6042, c.1904-07) and one dated 1909 with the low three-digit number 978. All are genuine period vitreous enamel on steel with the correct cobalt ground and white numerals -- the enamel loss shows base steel and old rust underneath rather than a modern repaint. Comfortably pre-1926 and catalogued to the year on the dated example. Low numbers are what the automobilia market pays for, and 978 is very low. Estimated $300-400 for three.

Problems. All three have enamel chipping -- the 12478 plate has significant loss along the lower centre and around the slots, the 6042 has losses at the top edge. Condition is what separates a $150 early plate from a $500 one, and these are mid-grade. Grouped as three, so you cannot cherry-pick the 1909. Automobilia is a collector market with no overlap with the rest of this collection.

ART NOUVEAU ALVIN SILVER OVERLAY GREEN GLASS VASE

This is the real thing. The photographs show a genuine period Alvin silver overlay on green glass with a ginkgo-and-whiplash design, and the base carries an impressed pattern number reading V1084C alongside the remains of a sterling mark. The overlay is chased with fine engraved detail in the leaf fans rather than being flat cast, and the glass is full of small seed bubbles consistent with turn-of-the-century production. Alvin overlay is authentic American Art Nouveau -- criterion three, cleanly met, at a price the real French names never reach.

Problems. Height is still unresolved and it matters more than anything else here: the photographs are shot against seamless white with no scale reference, which is exactly how a small vase is made to look large. Twelve-to-fourteen inch examples ask well over $3,000; a four-and-a-half inch one is a couple of hundred. Measure it at preview before bidding. Also check the overlay edges for lifting and the glass beneath for hairlines.

The William Marples Ultimatum brace is the most collected hand tool in the English-speaking world -- brass-framed, ebony-infilled, stamped with the Ultimatum registration, and bought by tool collectors who do not care what else is in the sale. It is a named maker, comfortably antique, and it sits in the budget band.

An early 19th-century painted box with secret drawers at a $200-300 estimate is one of the better value propositions in Day 1. It is catalogued as early 19th century, so the house has committed; painted surface and interior contrivance are both things the folk-art market pays for; and the estimate is a fraction of what a comparable box makes when it is described as folk art rather than as a box.

Problems. Original paint versus later repaint is the whole game. Period paint shows wear where hands went, shrinkage cracks that run through the colour rather than over it, and dirt in the crevices; repaint sits on top and is uniformly bright in the corners. Check the drawers actually work and are original to the box.

Stow Wengenroth is the finest American black-and-white lithographer of the twentieth century and the one printmaker in this sale whose Maine subjects are genuinely collected outside the state. Nine of his lithographs run consecutively here as lots 1308 to 1316, all estimated $600-800 with $250 openings. Nine at once is a consignment, and consignments of this size routinely exhaust the two or three people in the room who want them -- the last few in a run are where the value is.

Problems. Wengenroth editions were typically 250 impressions, so these are not rare, and the estimate band is optimistic for the weaker subjects. Check the margins for a pencil signature -- Wengenroth signed in pencil below the image, and an unsigned trial or a later restrike is worth a fraction. Look also for light-staining and mat burn, which are endemic in mid-century prints that have hung in Maine cottages.

An original plate is a genuine 17th-century object, which makes this potentially the oldest work on paper in the sale and comfortably the cheapest way to own something from before 1700.

Problems. Besler plates were reprinted in 1640 and 1713 from the same copperplates, and modern facsimiles are abundant. Look for a plate mark impressed into heavy laid paper, chain lines, and hand colouring that sits unevenly on the surface. Original sheets are large -- roughly 22 by 18 inches -- so a small sheet is a reproduction. Five photographs.

Rosecraft Hexagon dates c.1924-25, which puts it right on the 1926 line -- 'border', not 'antique'. Good Arts and Crafts form and the most attractive Roseville shape in this sale.

Problems. The estimate is the trap the brief already names. Roseville corrected hard and has not recovered; Rosecraft Hexagon gate vases sell $175-350, not $400-600. Check the base for a hairline running up from the foot -- the gate form is structurally weak at the bridge joins -- and check the bridge cut-out for a restored break, which is the standard damage on this shape and is easy to miss under matte glaze.

Lot 2305Day 2

INLAID MAHOGANY TEA CADDY WITH MIXING BOWL

c.1800-1830 · Inferred · antique
Ceramics & vasesGeorgian / 18th c.True antique
BUY IF CHEAP

An inlaid mahogany tea caddy with its mixing bowl. The mixing bowl is the point: most Georgian caddies lost their central cut-glass bowl within a generation, and a surviving original roughly doubles the piece. If the inlay and the carcase are period c.1800-1830 this is a genuine antique object with a real use-history. Estimated $600-800.

Problems. Caddies are among the most convincingly faked Georgian small furniture -- Edwardian and 1920s revival caddies use the same woods and stringing, and modern Indian-made 'Georgian' caddies are everywhere. Judge it on the interior: period caddies show oxidised, unfinished secondary wood, hand-cut dovetails at the corners, and lead-lined or foil-lined compartments with genuine tea staining. Confirm the mixing bowl is original to the caddy and not a later cut-glass replacement dropped in -- an original will fit its well exactly and show matching wear. Estimate is at the top of the band before any of that is verified.

Catalogued as a 'Lille 1737' faience platter. It is not a 1737 platter. 'Lille 1737' is a retro-mark used by late-19th-century French faience decorators, and everything visible here says c.1875-1900: an oval scallop-edged platter, a tavern scene inscribed D'APRES TENIERS -- after Teniers, which by the standing principle means copy -- signed H. Clerc (the catalogue reads it as M. Clerc), and a rim of ribbon-tied rose and forget-me-not swags in the sweet Boulenger-Montereau manner. Note that lot 1153 is a Boulenger & Cie, Montereau plaque by another hand; these two are almost certainly the same consignment. Still a genuine antique, still hand-painted, but the date on the mark is decoration.

Problems. The 1737 date in the title is the trap: anyone bidding on it as an 18th-century piece is paying four times what it is. Crazing throughout the glaze. It is displayed on a wire plate hanger whose arms are visible over the rim -- check what the wire has done to the glaze at the contact points. 'After Teniers' means this is a copy of a copy: a 19th-c. faience painter working from an engraving after a 17th-c. painting.

An Iznik blue and white bowl at $600-800. The first of a four-lot Ottoman group (2431, 2434, 2436, 2438). Late Iznik and its Kutahya successors are genuinely 17th-century and satisfy the age criterion better than almost anything else in the sale, but they need to be told apart from the 19th-century revival ware -- Theodore Deck, late Kutahya and Turkish tourist production -- which copies the same designs on a clean white body with bright, stable colours.

Problems. Condition is the whole question in this group. Iznik of this date is almost never found undamaged, and dishes far more often than bowls. Get the piece under a light and look for filled breaks and overpainted rim losses; restoration on Islamic pottery is often extensive and skilfully hidden. At $600-800 the estimate leaves no room for a restoration discount.

A Turkish Iznik dish, and this one the photograph does settle on period: the palette has degraded exactly the way late Iznik does -- the Armenian bole red has gone brown-black and sits proud of the surface, the greens have muddied, the cobalt has softened into the glaze -- and the body is a warm off-white rather than the bright clean white of 19th-century revival ware. A stylised rock-and-wave or saz-leaf rim band with a small green-and-yellow medallion at the centre. Genuinely 17th century, genuinely in the spirit of the age criterion.

Problems. It is broken. The photograph shows long radiating cracks running from the centre out through the cavetto and into the rim on at least four axes -- this dish has been broken and reassembled, or is holding together on a stable but total network of breaks. There is heavy rim chipping and glaze loss around the edge. That is normal for the type and it is why the estimate is $600-800 rather than several thousand, but it caps what this can ever be worth and it is not a piece to bid up on the period alone.

Lot 1017Day 1

MAHOGANY SHAPED TILT TOP CANDLESTAND

c.1790-1820 or c.1900-1920 · Unverified · border
Furniture & boxesUndeterminedTrue antique
CHECK FIRST
key lot

Thomaston has not dated this at all -- the title is pure description, which is itself the tell. A mahogany tilt-top candlestand with a shaped top is the single most reproduced form in American furniture: the Colonial Revival made thousands between 1890 and 1930 that copy the Federal originals closely. The photographs show a snake-foot tripod base and a well-figured shaped top, but nothing in them settles the century.

Problems. The whole question is period versus revival, and it is a 130-year spread on the same object. Look underneath at preview: hand-cut irregular saw marks, an off-centre lathe hole, oxidised unfinished surfaces and shrinkage out-of-round all say period. Circular saw marks anywhere say 1830 at the earliest and in practice mean revival. A crisp machine-flat underside is the giveaway.
My market estimate$250 - $600
If you resold it$150 - $420
Margin at target+$161

Why the range is wide. The range is the whole problem: period Federal at the top, Colonial Revival at the bottom, same object.

Thomaston has committed to an 1846 N. Currier imprint, which is a claim you can hold the house to, and the Boston Tea Party is a desirable subject. The trouble is that the Currier images are the most reproduced in American printmaking -- calendar reissues, Travelers Insurance giveaways and 1930s facsimiles run into the millions, and many carry the original imprint line because it was part of the image being copied.

Problems. The whole verdict turns on process, and this is exactly what looking at the sheet settles. A period hand-coloured lithograph shows a continuous greasy tone with visible stone grain and watercolour sitting on the surface in uneven washes. A facsimile shows a regular dot rosette under magnification and colour that registers too perfectly. Take a loupe to the preview. Also check for trimmed margins, which kill the value of an original.

Two albums and a metal box of postcards is a lottery ticket whose value is entirely in the contents. Real-photo postcards of named midcoast towns -- Bath, Wiscasset, Waldoboro, Rockland waterfronts, shipyards, launchings -- sell $10 to $50 each, so a single album with fifty good Maine RPPCs justifies the whole estimate several times over. Two albums of European tourist views and printed greetings is a $60 lot.

Problems. The two photographs show the albums closed and the box shut, which tells you nothing. This is the single most preview-dependent lot in Day 1: you must open them. Real-photo cards have a matte photographic surface and a stamp box printed with AZO, VELOX or similar; printed cards show a dot screen under a loupe.

MARK CATESBY (SC/ENGLAND, 1683-1749)

Mark Catesby's Natural History of Carolina plates are genuine 18th-century hand-coloured etchings and among the founding works of American natural history illustration. A real Catesby plate is comfortably antique and a named-maker hit, and $400-600 is a plausible price for a modest subject.

Problems. The 1754 and 1771 editions are period; the 1974 Beehive Press facsimiles and various 20th-century reproductions are not, and they are common. Check for a plate mark impressed into the paper, laid paper with visible chain lines, and hand-colouring that sits unevenly on the surface. A sheet with no plate impression is a reproduction regardless of what the frame says.

Lot 1407Day 1

CHINESE 'CARP' PORCELAIN PLAQUE ATTRIBUTED TO DENG BISHAN (CHINA, 1874-1930)

CHECK FIRST

A Chinese porcelain carp plaque attributed to Deng Bishan (1874-1930). Deng Bishan was a real and significant Jingdezhen porcelain painter of the Republic period, in the circle around the Eight Friends of Zhushan, and a genuine signed plaque by him is a five-figure object. This is estimated $300-400. That gap is the whole story: the house has written 'attributed to' and then priced it as a decorative plaque, which is the house telling you what it actually thinks. Per the standing principle on estimates an order of magnitude below a genuine work, believe the estimate, not the name.

Problems. Deng Bishan is among the most forged of the Republic-period painters; signed carp plaques in his manner are produced in quantity in Jingdezhen today and sold openly. Establishing a real one needs a specialist reading of the calligraphy, the seal, the enamel quality and the frame. My market range spans more than tenfold, which is unresolved attribution rather than value -- that is why no margin is shown. If you like the picture, buy it as an anonymous Republic-style plaque at $200-300 and treat any upside as a lottery ticket.
My market estimate$200 - $3,000
If you resold it$140 - $2,000

Why the range is wide. The range is an attribution question, not a valuation. A genuine Deng Bishan plaque and a Jingdezhen plaque signed in his name are the same object to a photograph and an order of magnitude apart in value. No margin is shown because averaging that spread would be inventing a number.

A 16th-century oak child's chair at $400-600 is either the most remarkable value in the entire sale or it is not what the catalogue says. Genuine 16th-century seating furniture of any kind is museum material; a child's chair from that date surviving in usable condition would normally carry four figures at minimum. Seven photographs suggests the house is showing it thoroughly, which is a good sign.

Problems. The estimate is the problem. When a house catalogues something to the 16th century and then estimates it at $400, the estimate is telling you what the specialists actually think. Assume heavy restoration, substantial replacement, or a much later date -- 17th or 18th century oak is routinely optimistically catalogued. Examine the joints for replaced pegs, the seat for renewal, and the overall surface for the deep, hard, almost black patina that genuinely early oak develops.

Lot 3009Day 3

PIERRE JULES MENE (FRANCE, 1810-1879)

19th c. cast or later recast · Inferred · border
Sculpture & bronzesVictorian / 19th c.Named makerTrue antique
CHECK FIRST

Pierre-Jules Mene is the most commercially successful of the French animalier sculptors and this is the pick of the Day 3 bronze run on price -- $600-800 against Barye at $1,000-2,000. A genuine period Mene sand cast is a real named-maker antique and would be excellent value at this money.

Problems. That is exactly why the category is a minefield. Mene's models were recast continuously after his death in 1879 and again through the 20th century, and later casts carry the same signature because it is cast into the model. The tells are in the chasing and the surface: period casts show crisp hand-finished detail in the fur and mane, a rich layered patina that varies with the form, and a smooth well-finished underside. Late casts are soft in the detail, uniformly dark, and often rough or unfinished underneath. Check for a foundry mark and weigh it in your hand -- period sand casts are heavier than they look.

Problems. Elephant ivory is subject to federal Endangered Species Act restrictions on interstate commerce and to documentation requirements that the auction house is unlikely to supply. WASHINGTON MINT YEAR 2000 GIANT QUARTER-POUND GOLDEN PROOF SILVER MEDALLION

2000 · Catalogued · modern
Silver & goldContemporaryPrecious metal
PASS

The photographs confirm the trap exactly as flagged. This is a Washington Mint gilt silver Sacagawea medallion in its original presentation box and capsule -- a private-mint bullion novelty from 2000 with no numismatic standing whatsoever. The gold colour is a plated surface, not gold content, and the word 'golden' in the title is doing dishonest work.

Problems. A quarter pound is 113 grams, about 3.6 troy ounces, which is roughly $182 of silver at the working spot and less after a refiner discounts a plated piece. The estimate of $300-500 is nearly triple the metal. When the estimate exceeds melt on a modern bullion item, the estimate is the trap, not the opportunity. The box shows foxing and spotting, which tells you how these were stored and how many survive.

Lot 1131Day 1

PR KATHODIAN BRONZE WORKS COWBOY BOOKENDS

c.1925-1935 · Inferred · modern
Sculpture & bronzesArt Deco / 1920s-30s
PASS

Kathodian Bronze Works bookends are not bronze in any useful sense. The company made thin metal shells over composition or plaster cores and finished them to look like cast bronze, and the name was chosen to encourage exactly the confusion the catalogue title now reproduces. Cowboy subjects are common in the line.

Problems. The tell is weight and the sound: solid bronze is heavy and rings, a clad shell is light and thuds. Check the underside for the composition core showing through, and for chips at the edges where the shell has separated. Even in perfect condition these are $60-120 objects.

Lot 1164Day 1

ANDREW WYETH (AMERICAN, 1917–2009), COLLOGRAPH PRINT, "END OF OLSON'S"

1993 · Catalogued · modern
Prints & works on paperContemporaryMaine coastal
PASS
key lot

This one is resolved, and the answer overturns the working hypothesis. The margin does not say collotype and 'collograph' is not a typo -- the sheet carries a printed trademark banner reading 'A COLLOGRAPH Print', which is a brand name, and beneath it the line '(c) 1993 Aaron Ashley Inc., Yonkers, N.Y.' with 'Made in U.S.A.' Aaron Ashley is a commercial fine-art reproduction publisher. The title, the artist's name and the 'Collection of Rosalie H. Levine' credit are all printed in the margin as part of the sheet.

Problems. There is no pencil signature, no edition number, no publisher of record in the print world's sense, and no date before 1993. This is not the authorised Triton or Aristo collotype and it should not be priced anywhere near one -- the $1,000-2,000 collotype comps are simply the wrong comparison. It is a 1990s photomechanical reproduction of End of Olson's worth $50-100, and in this case the frame and glass may genuinely be worth more than the print inside them.
My market estimate$50 - $110
If you resold it$20 - $70

Why the range is wide. A 1993 Aaron Ashley commercial reproduction. The frame and glass may be the more valuable half of the lot.

A scrimshawed whale's tooth with whaling subject -- one of five whale's teeth in Day 1 (1285, 1287, 1289, 1296 plus 1292). Genuine period scrimshaw is desirable, but this whole group carries the same two problems.

Problems. First, authenticity: modern polymer resin fakes and 1960s kit-scrimshaw (see lot 1283 in this very sale) are endemic, and the tells -- too-white material, no dentine grain, engraving that sits on rather than in the surface -- need a loupe. Second, the legal constraint: sperm whale teeth are Marine Mammal Protection Act material, and while a pre-Act piece bought in-state at a Maine sale is the simplest case, it restricts everything afterwards. Not worth the friction at this price.

Problems. 'Celadon jade' should mean nephrite, but the term is used loosely and the same descriptions cover serpentine, bowenite and dyed quartzite. Carved dragon bangles are made in enormous quantity in modern China. Distinguishing nephrite needs specific gravity and a refractometer, not a photograph -- this is a preview or gemmologist question and there is no melt-style floor to fall back on. At $660-924 all-in it is at the top of the band with the material itself unverified.

Stones. Diamond and sapphire in a Deco ring. Secondary-market recovery on small stones is 25-40% of retail at best, and period sapphires are frequently heat-treated. The Deco design is worth more than the stones.

Ceramics & vasesVictorian / 19th c.True antiquemaker
PASS

Six Russian Imperial Porcelain Factory soup plates, Alexander II period. The reverse photograph settles it: a green underglaze crowned cypher mark of the Alexander II type with a date, which is the correct factory mark for 1855-1881. The faces carry a gilt-and-red crowned monogram. This is the best-documented ceramic lot in the sale -- the highest-status porcelain factory in Europe, a reign-dated mark, and genuine imperial service ware. It is also $1,000-1,500, which is $1,320-1,980 all-in and out of the band. If it stalls under $1,000 in the room it becomes interesting; do not plan on it.

Problems. Above budget. There is a stained or restored area on the foot ring of the plate photographed from beneath -- check all six. The front cypher is hard to read at photograph resolution and does not obviously match an Alexander II monogram; the backstamp is the authority, but reconcile the two at preview before paying imperial money. IPF marks are forged, though usually on higher-value pieces than soup plates.

A 14K gold opal and diamond ring at $500-700 sits inside the budget, which makes it worth a specific warning rather than a silent screen.

Problems. The brief's standing point applies directly: composite and doublet opals are worth far less relative to their gold content than solid stones, and a ring at this price with a substantial opal is a strong candidate for a doublet. Under magnification a doublet shows a flat join line at the girdle. The gold in a ring of this size is perhaps 3 to 5 grams -- $225 to $375 -- so the estimate assumes the stone carries real value. Verify the opal is solid before treating any of that as real.

The first of eleven Andrew Wyeth lots in Day 3 (3469-3479), estimated $1,000-3,000 and none of them naming a process. Day 1 carried twenty-six more. This is the same structural trap the brief identifies, one day later and at triple the estimates.

Problems. Lot 1164 in Day 1 has now been proved a 1993 Aaron Ashley commercial reproduction despite a catalogue description that implied a hand process. Nothing here names a medium, an edition or a date. Out of band anyway at $1,000-2,000, but the wider point is that eleven consecutive unspecified Wyeths should be read as a consignment of reproductions until each is individually proved otherwise.

The category-level PASS reasons

Every lot in the sale has a verdict. The ones marked PASS as a compact row got that verdict from one of the reasons below rather than from an individual write-up — a reasoned call applied to a lot that clearly fits an identified pattern. They carry no value estimates, because I will not put a number on something I have not costed individually. Say which category to deepen next and those rows become full write-ups with market, resale and melt figures, exactly as the jewellery now has.

Reviewed and set aside111

Looked at, no criteria fit and nothing in the title or estimate to argue for a second look. Listed so the coverage is visible rather than silently missing.

Above the budget band65

Estimated at $1,000 hammer and up, which is $1,320 all-in before the bidding starts. Some of this is excellent material -- the Rockland sternboard, the Federal furniture, the period portraits -- but bidding here means abandoning the discipline that makes the rest of the list work.

Firearms, optics and sporting42

Roughly fifty consecutive Day 1 lots of shotguns, rifles, scopes, knives and decoys. Outside all five criteria, and the transfer paperwork makes them a poor fit for a collection bought at a Maine sale. A handful are genuinely pre-1899 but none is what this buyer is after.

Oriental rugs and carpets39

Thirty-plus Day 2 rugs. Deep continuous supply at every sale in New England, no criteria fit, and condition on decorative carpets is impossible to judge from catalogue photographs.

Chinese and Asian decorative34

Around a hundred lots of Chinese porcelain, jade, robes and export ware across Days 1 and 2. Mostly late Qing to Republic period or later, decorative rather than antique by this brief's standard, and a category where reproduction is endemic and unverifiable from photographs.

Books, documents and ephemera32

Volumes, sets, maps and documents beyond the handful written up individually. A deep category where condition and collation decide everything and neither is visible in a catalogue photograph.

Maine artists reviewed, not pursued19

The Day 3 Maine section runs to well over a hundred lots. These are the ones where the artist is genuinely Maine-associated but the lot fails on price, on being a contemporary gallery-priced living painter, or on being an oil where the same artist's works on paper are the affordable way in. The brief's Maine allowance is a reason to look, not a reason to buy.

Decorative copper, brass and dinnerware17

The Day 1 copper cookware run, brass preserve pans, and dinnerware in quantity. All three are named in the brief as weak markets, and the copper consignment in particular is fifteen-plus lots of the same thing.

Ivory and marine-mammal material15

Whale's teeth, walrus tusk, sailor-made ivory and carved elephant ivory. Federal Endangered Species Act and Marine Mammal Protection Act rules restrict what can be done with these afterwards, and the paperwork will not accompany lots at this price. Set aside as a class -- see the standing note below the filters.

Toys, dolls and holiday decorations14

The Day 1 toy and Halloween runs. Some is genuinely pre-1926 and the Halloween material has a real collecting base, but none of it touches the five criteria and condition dominates value in ways photographs cannot settle.

Listed painters, no criteria fit9

Catalogued as a name with dates and nothing else -- no medium, no subject, no date on the work. Most are competent regional or European painters with thin comparable records, none has a Maine connection, and the boilerplate biographies attached to these lots are indexing, not provenance.

Victorian and later furniture8

Eastlake, upholstered Victorian, mid-century and reproduction case furniture. The brief names this as a standing weak market and nothing here argues for an exception.

Anonymous portraits and period paintings8

Unsigned and unattributed portraits, genre scenes and landscapes. The brief names anonymous 19th-century child portraits specifically as a weak market, and the wider category has the same problem: genuinely old, genuinely anonymous, and priced as though the age alone carried it.

Vehicles, machinery and modern sporting goods8

Cars, a kayak, a log-splitter, a food trailer and similar. Self-evidently outside the brief.

Wyeth reproduction blocks7

Twenty-six Wyeth lots across Day 1 (1158-1172, 1430-1440) from consignors offering reproductions under the most famous name in Maine painting. Lot 1164 has now been proved a 1993 Aaron Ashley commercial print, which sets the standard for the rest of the run.

Samplers, coverlets and needlework7

Period textiles beyond the examples written up. Condition dominates value here and it is exactly what a catalogue photograph cannot show -- fading, restitching and remounting are all invisible until the piece is in your hands.

Roseville, Steuben and art glass4

Both names are called out in the brief as markets whose estimates run ahead of reality -- they corrected hard and have not recovered -- and Roseville is the most reproduced American art pottery there is. Tiffany Studios is here too, at $1,500 to $35,000, which is simply another budget.

Walking canes and sticks3

The Day 1 cane consignment. Cane collecting rewards mechanism, gadget and figural carving, none of which is claimed for any of these, and the gold-filled mounts on lot 1026 have no melt floor at all.

Marine fittings, models and instruments2

Half hulls, telescopes, ship models, deck clocks, flags, rigging blocks and hand-painted ship replicas. Genuinely on-theme for the coastal brief, and the best of it is written up -- these are the remainder, where the object is either undated, a modern decorative replica, or priced above what a fitting of that kind returns.
